notes.meaning: Bildad from Shuah steps forward as the second friend to answer Job. He agrees with the first speaker, Eliphaz, but speaks with a harsher tone. He believes strongly that God deals with people strictly based on what they deserve.

Bildad scolds Job for talking so much and calls his speeches a blustering wind. He thinks Job is letting strong anger run wild instead of accepting his punishment quietly. To Bildad, Job's loud complaints are both empty and dangerous.

Bildad asks whether God could ever twist what is fair and right. Since the Almighty needs nothing from human beings, He has no reason to cheat or act unfairly. Bildad is right that God is just, but he wrongly assumes that all suffering is a penalty for personal sin.

Bildad harshly suggests that Job's children died because they had sinned against God. He claims God simply handed them over to the destructive power of their own rebellion. This cruel statement cut deep into a grieving father who had regularly offered sacrifices for his children.

Bildad tells Job that there is still hope for him if he seeks God without delay. Instead of complaining, Job should go directly to the Almighty and beg for mercy. Bildad urges him to turn his grief into earnest prayer.

Bildad promises that if Job is truly pure and honest, God will quickly step in to rescue him. God would then rebuild Job's home and make his life peaceful again. By saying 'if,' Bildad hints that Job's ongoing misery proves his heart is not actually clean.

Bildad assures Job that even if his new start is tiny, his future will end up far greater than before. Though Bildad spoke with a doubtful heart, his words turned out to be an accurate prophecy of Job's final restoration. God often begins with small things before pouring out great blessings.

differ.view: Some Baptists see here a picture of Christian growth, where a small start in faith gradually develops into a rich and fruitful spiritual life.

notes.meaning: Bildad urges Job to look back into history and study what the earliest fathers discovered. Instead of relying on his own ideas, Job should learn from long ages of human experience. Bildad trusts that ancient tradition will prove his point about God's justice.

Bildad reminds Job that living people were born only yesterday and know very little on their own. Human life moves swiftly and vanishes like a fleeting shadow. Because our days are so short, we must rely on the wisdom gathered across centuries.

Bildad says the ancient elders will teach Job true understanding. They do not give thoughtless opinions, but speak from sincere reflection and long-tested knowledge. Bildad prepares Job to hear old proverbs about what happens to the wicked.

Bildad quotes an old nature riddle, asking if water reeds or papyrus plants can grow without wet mud. These tall plants need constant water to stay alive and thrive. In the same way, human beings cannot truly flourish without God's ongoing favor.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars point out that the words for reed and papyrus are borrowed from Egyptian, indicating that Bildad is drawing on famous wisdom sayings from the Nile region.

notes.meaning: While still green and before anyone cuts it down, a water reed quickly dries up if the moisture is gone. It withers faster than ordinary grass because it has no inner strength without the swamp. This shows how quickly an ungodly person's success can vanish overnight.

Bildad explains that this is what happens to everyone who forgets God. A hypocrite, someone who only pretends to be godly on the outside, will see his hopes completely wiped out. A religion with no real heart will dry up when hard times arrive.

The false hope of an ungodly person is as weak as a spider's web. A spider spins its home with great effort out of its own body, yet the thinnest breeze can break it. A person who trusts in wealth or good deeds has built on nothing stronger than a cobweb.

The sinner tries to lean on his web-like house for security, but it collapses beneath him. He tries to hold on tight to his family, money, and reputation, but none of them can keep him standing. A false refuge always fails when real trouble strikes.

Bildad gives another picture from nature, describing a rank weed spreading out in the sunshine. It looks juicy and green, creeping easily across the whole garden. It seems so strong and healthy that nobody expects it to die.

differ.view: Some Anglicans understand verses 16 and 17 as a contrast describing a godly person who truly flourishes, rather than another picture of a doomed sinner.

notes.meaning: The plant wraps its roots tightly around a heap of stones, looking like it has claimed a solid rock house. A wealthy sinner often thinks he is completely safe because his riches seem grounded on solid rock. Yet earthly security is only an illusion.

When God tears the plant away from its spot, the very ground acts as if it never saw it. The plant disappears so completely that no trace of it is left behind. When a proud sinner falls, the world forgets him just as fast.

Bildad uses bitter sarcasm to say that this ruin is all the 'joy' a sinner ever gets. His proud lifestyle ends in nothing, and other plants spring up from the dirt to take his place. Human pride is easily wiped out and quickly replaced.

Bildad summarizes his main point by declaring that God never casts off a truly blameless person. He also insists that God will never take evildoers by the hand to help them along. While God certainly protects His people, Bildad wrongly assumes that Job's pain means God has rejected him.

Bildad promises that if Job repents, God will once again fill his mouth with laughter and glad shouting. He believes that true joy always follows sincere repentance. Although Bildad doubted Job's goodness, God really did bring Job back to joy in the end.

Bildad finishes his speech by saying that Job's enemies will be covered with shame when Job is restored. Meanwhile, the homes of wicked people will vanish into nothing. Bildad wants to encourage Job, but his rigid ideas still hurt his suffering friend.
